messages.subject: Re: Iterations required for n=2500
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for attaching those—it looks like things converge quite well for the subset, at least for these parameters. It makes me wonder if either:

1) there are particular subjects in the larger sample that have poor convergence,
2) there are multiple subgroups in the data that lead to some sort of convergence issue, or
3) the model parameterization is making it difficult for the sampler to explore certain regions of the parameter space

To determine which of these may be happening, once you have the full dataset fit, it would be helpful to see those traceplots in addition to perhaps some pairs plots on the group-level parameters. You can look at pairs plots by doing something like:

pairs(my_fit$fit, pars = c("mu_phi", "mu_eta", "mu_gam", "mu_tau", "sigma"))

This should help locate divergences, which will be highlighted in the scatterplots. If they are concentrated in certain regions of the scatterplot, it could indicate where the sampler is having trouble.

Best,
Nate

messages.subject: Re: Warning message about the value of pareto k
messages.subject_clean: Warning message about the value of pareto k
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ni,

Thanks for your interest!

So, the reason we get these warnings is related to how we are computing the log likelihood for each participant. Instead of saving the likelihood for each trial, we sum over the trials within participants, and then compute LOOIC on the resulting participant by MCMC sample matrix. The rationale is that this measure is an approximation to a leave one participant out score, rather than a leave one trial out score.

The problem seems to come up because, for some tasks/models, participants very quite a bit on how well the model captures their choices, causing the importance sampling procedure used to estimate LOO to produce high pareto K diagnostics, which indicate that the LOOIC estimate may not be reliable. There are some details on this exact problem here: https://groups.google.com/g/stan-users/c/kew2-ODKYwQ/m/UBJ1JEiBAQAJ. Overall, the ideal solution is to perform an actual leave-one-participant out cross validation procedure, but this can be rather computationally intensive and we do not have a default functionality for it in the package at the moment. Another solution is to modify the stan code to keep the trial-level likelihood and compute LOOIC on the resulting matrix, but this changes the interpretation a bit. In my own experience, such a change does remedy the pareto k diagnostics, and I have found that both tend to identify the same model as "best", although I am sure this will depend on the model/task/data.

In my opinion, the best approach in this case is to treat the model comparison more comprehensively—e.g., do posterior predictive checks, parameter recovery analyses, or whatever else, and the LOOIC metric is then just another metric to use to help determine which model is best for your given problem. Ideally, you could also perform other types of cross validation checks. We are still thinking about a  more general solution, but hopefully the above can be helpful for now.

Best,
Nate

messages.subject: Coding softmax choice rule for a subset of bandits
messages.subject_clean: Coding softmax choice rule for a subset of bandits
messages.body_plain:
Hi team, this is my first time posting -- any advice you are able to offer is greatly appreciated!

I'm working on custom .stan and .R codes for a bandit task based off of a few hBayesDM .stan files. I'm fitting a (model-free) temporal-difference RL model to task behavior. In each trial of the task, the agent chooses between 2 out of a set of bandits (let's say N = 4 bandits), and I'm trying different approaches to coding a softmax choice function over the 2 options presented on each trial. My goal is to code the choice function in a manner that only incorporates the two options on each trial as variables, and leaves the unobserved bandits on each trial out of the equation. In essence, I do not want the values of the options that are not shown on each trial to influence the softmax calculation of the values of the options that are presented on each trial.

At present, I'm using a "choice[i, t] ~ categorical_logit( Q-values * tau[i])" line in the Model section, and correspondingly a "choice[i, t] ~ categorical_logit_lpmf( Q-values * tau[i] )" line in the Generated Quantities section, where choice[i, t] (int<lower=1, upper=4) is the chosen bandit by participant [i] on each trial [t], Q-values is a N=4 component vector of learned action values derived from the TDRL model, and tau is a temperature parameter. However, I do not want the categorical_logit model to use all 4 values of the Q-values vector, but instead to use only the Q-values of the 2 options presented on each trial (which will be some random pairing of the 4 possible bandits).

Is the categorical_logit model the best route for this setup? Since the choices are coded as integers 1:4, I've been using a 4-component vector the store the Q-values. Is it more sensible to re-code the choices to something that would work with a bernoulli_logit model (i.e., having the option on the left be choice=1, and the right be choice=0)? I think working up a way to escape the categorical labels (i.e., integer bandit indexing) would obviate the need to use the 4-component vector and instead I could use a 2-component vector for calculating a softmax choice between the 2 options on each trial. Could someone check me on this thinking?

Thanks for reading!
Paul Sands

messages.subject: Re: Coding softmax choice rule for a subset of bandits
messages.subject_clean: Coding softmax choice rule for a subset of bandits
messages.body_plain:
hi Paul,

I once encountered similar situations and the idea is to create some helping variables. See below.

In an example where options 2 and 3 are presented as stimuli, and the participant chose 2, then,

data {
...
  int<lower=1, upper=4> chosen[N, T];   // option 2 in this case
  int<lower=1, upper=4> unchosen[N, T]; // option 3 in this case
...
}

model {
...
  vector[4] Q_values;
  vector[2] Q_presented;

  Q_presented[1] = Q_values[chosen[i,t]];  // here 1/2 indices need to corresponde the button presses
  Q_presented[2] = Q_values[unchosen[i,t]];

  choice[i, t] ~ categorical_logit( tau[i] * Q_presented); // choice here 1/2
...
}

Hope that helps,
Lei

Thanks very much for providing all the practical advice.

I have restarted the model fitting using 4000 iterations (n=2512) so that I could investigate the traceplots and pairplots that you mentioned quicker.
This time, the traceplots and pairplots look as below:

And the system messages said that:
1: There were 2289 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.95 may help.
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
3: The largest R-hat is 1.57, indicating chains have not mixed.
Running the chains for more iterations may help.
4: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
Running the chains for more iterations may help.
5: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
Running the chains for more iterations may help.

I am sorry for the information overload but would be much appreciated if further advice could be given with regard to the model-fitting procedure - would increasing the adapt_delta to 0.99 solve the convergence problem?

Many Thanks and Kind Regards
Crystal

messages.body_plain:
Hi Crystal,

The model did not converge at all. As Nate suggested, why don't you try the model with a smaller number of subjects like 20 or 30 first? And what do you mean by "...4000 iterations (n=2512)"? As we noted in the hBayesDM paper (Ahn et al., 2017, Computational Psychiatry), assuming a single hyper-group might be too strong if using a large number of subjects.

Best,
Young

messages.body_plain:
Following up with Young's comment—yes it looks like you have some bimodalities in the posterior, which could arise for a variety of reasons. I see that some of the parameters are up against the bounds (i.e. right at 0), so perhaps some less diffuse priors would be useful, although this would require modifying the Stan code.

It is also rather interesting that all the divergences are happening in one of the modes (the red dots are in specific clouds in the pairs plots), which may indicate that certain parts of the parameter space are problematic. It is possible that changed adapt_delta could help a bit, and also perhaps setting different initial values to see if the same pattern arises in the posterior.

Best,
Nate

Hi Crystal,

The model did not converge at all. As Nate suggested, why don't you try the model with a smaller number of subjects like 20 or 30 first? And what do you mean by "...4000 iterations (n=2512)"? As we noted in the hBayesDM paper (Ahn et al., 2017, Computational Psychiatry), assuming a single hyper-group might be too strong if using a large number of subjects.

Best,
Young
